item.title: Six Pitfalls Implementing HNSW: A Debug Journal from 0% to 98%+ Recall
item.author: xxxx
item.description: While implementing the HNSW algorithm for my vector database project vex (initial code AI-assisted, debugging and optimization done by hand), I ran my first Recall test — every single metric was 0%. Not 50%, not 30%. Zero. The HNSW results and BruteForce results had absolutely no overlap. This post documents the entire journey from 0% to 98%+ recall, cross-referencing each bug with the original HNSW paper.

item.title: Temporal Single-Node Reliability Deep Dive: How It Survives Server Crashes, Network Failures, and Rollback Errors
item.author: xxxx
item.description: Writing business logic with Temporal is pure joy — “code like a single-machine program, get distributed fault tolerance for free.” But after the honeymoon phase, a nagging question remains: Is it really reliable? What if the Server crashes? What about network partitions? What if the rollback itself fails? This article tears apart these questions from the ground up.

item.title: Temporal in Practice: From Saga Pattern to Self-Healing Distributed Transactions
item.author: xxxx
item.description: While building a trading system backend, I used Temporal to solve the classic distributed transaction consistency problem. This post breaks down Temporal’s core mechanisms and explores its applications in AI task scheduling.

item.title: NAS Disk Health Monitoring: From smartctl to Custom Agent
item.author: xxxx
item.description: A NAS’s most important job is protecting user data. Disk failures often have warning signs, and SMART technology can detect problems early. This post documents how to build a disk health monitoring agent.

item.title: Go Microservices War Stories: 5 Lessons from Dependency Management to Service Discovery
item.author: xxxx
item.description: Microservices isn’t just about splitting up a monolith. This post documents 5 real pitfalls I hit in Go microservices projects, and how to avoid them.

item.title: Building a Mini Filesystem: Custom FS with FUSE + Go
item.author: xxxx
item.description: The best way to learn filesystems is to write one yourself. This post uses FUSE + Go to implement an in-memory filesystem with basic read/write operations, deep-diving into core concepts like inode and block.
